claim: Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts published 'A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity' in the Bulletin of Mathematical Biophysics 5:115-133 (1943), idealising the neuron as an all-or-none threshold unit so that nets of them could be described by propositional logic.
McCulloch-Pitts nets did not learn: the paper's fifth assumption states 'The structure of the net does not change with time.'
The 1943 paper showed that a net furnished with a tape and scanners computes exactly what a Turing machine can; finite nets with loops alone compute only some of those numbers.
Every loop-free McCulloch-Pitts net can be described by a logical expression; the converse holds only for logical expressions 'satisfying certain conditions'.
The 1943 McCulloch-Pitts paper cites only three works: Carnap (1938), Hilbert & Ackermann (1927) and Whitehead & Russell's Principia Mathematica; no biology papers.
The 1943 paper's byline names the University of Illinois College of Medicine (Illinois Neuropsychiatric Institute) and the University of Chicago.
Pitts was about 18 and McCulloch 42 when Jerome Lettvin introduced them in Chicago around 1941; McCulloch took Pitts into his family home in Hinsdale, Illinois.

According to Amanda Gefter's account (after Conway & Siegelman), Pitts at about 12 read Principia Mathematica in a Detroit library in three days; the story of his letter to Russell and Russell's invitation is unverified biographical tradition.
Pitts never finished a doctorate; whether he held any degree at all is disputed (Smalheiser: none of any kind; Wikipedia citing Godel's Collected Works: a Chicago Associate of Arts).
Pitts came to MIT in the autumn of 1943 to work with Norbert Wiener (Wiener's own account).
The McCulloch-Pitts paper initially 'made barely a ripple among brain scientists'.
John von Neumann's June 1945 First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC modelled computer 'elements' on neurons, 'Following W. Pitts and W. S. MacCulloch' (sic); it is the draft's only citation.
The Macy conferences on cybernetics began on 8-9 March 1946 in New York, chaired by McCulloch, and ran ten meetings through 1953.

At the 7th Macy conference (23-24 March 1950) neurophysiologist Ralph Gerard argued the brain works in a far more analog than digital way, the main dissent inside cybernetics against the McCulloch-Pitts picture.
Norbert Wiener published Cybernetics: Or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine in 1948; it sold over 22,000 copies by the end of 1949 (per Kline, The Cybernetics Moment).

Seeing McCulloch's 1947 diagram for a reading machine for the blind, neuroanatomist Gerhardt von Bonin asked whether it was a diagram of the fourth layer of the visual cortex (as recounted by Wiener).
Donald Hebb's The Organization of Behavior (Wiley, 1949) states on p. 62 the postulate that when cell A repeatedly takes part in firing cell B, A's efficiency in firing B is increased.
'Neurons that fire together, wire together' is not Hebb's wording; it is a later paraphrase usually traced to Carla Shatz (1992).
Alan Turing's 1948 NPL report 'Intelligent Machinery' described randomly connected 'unorganised machines' of neuron-like units that could be trained; it went unpublished until 1968.

Turing's 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' (Mind 59(236):433-460, October 1950) proposed the imitation game, called 'Can machines think?' 'too meaningless to deserve discussion', and suggested building and educating a 'child machine'.
Turing proposed rewards and punishments for the child machine but wrote they 'can at best be a part of the teaching process'.

Turing predicted that in about fifty years computers with storage of about 10^9 would play the imitation game so well that an average interrogator would have no more than a 70 per cent chance of correct identification after five minutes.
Claude Shannon's maze-solving mouse Theseus (1950) used telephone relays under a 5x5 maze floor as memory; it was demonstrated at the 1951 Macy conference. It was relay memory, not a neural network.

In summer 1951 Marvin Minsky and Dean Edmonds built SNARC at Harvard: about 40 'neurons', 'three hundred tubes and a lot of motors', forty control knobs as memory turned by clutches driven by a surplus B-24 bomber gyropilot; ONR provided 'a couple of thousand dollars' via George Miller (Minsky's 1981 recollection).
SNARC's tube count is disputed: Minsky recalled about 300 tubes; the AIMA textbook says 3,000. Minsky's own figure is preferred.
Minsky's 1954 Princeton PhD thesis was 'Theory of Neural-Analog Reinforcement Systems and Its Application to the Brain-Model Problem'.

The Dartmouth proposal by McCarthy, Minsky, Rochester and Shannon, dated 31 August 1955, introduced the term 'artificial intelligence' and proposed 'a 2 month, 10 man study' on the conjecture that every aspect of learning could be precisely described so a machine could simulate it.
'Neuron Nets' was explicitly topic 3 of the Dartmouth proposal, and Minsky's bio in it notes he 'has built a machine for simulating learning by nerve nets'.
The Dartmouth organisers requested $13,500; the Rockefeller Foundation granted $7,500.

The Dartmouth summer's length is given variously as five weeks (Rockefeller Foundation), six (traditional) or eight (Solomonoff/More notes, about 18 June to 17 August 1956); 'one summer, about two months' is safe.
Attendance at Dartmouth was patchy: only McCarthy, Minsky and Solomonoff stayed throughout; Newell and Simon were expected only for the first two weeks.
McCarthy later wrote that one reason for inventing the term 'artificial intelligence' was to escape association with cybernetics and to avoid accepting Norbert Wiener as a guru or arguing with him.

Newell, Simon and Shaw's Logic Theorist was hand-simulated in January 1956, printed its first JOHNNIAC proof in August 1956, and proved 38 of the first 52 theorems of Principia chapter 2 in runs of late 1956-1957; it was not running on a computer while Newell and Simon were at Dartmouth.
Rochester, Holland, Haibt and Duda's IBM 704 simulation testing Hebb's cell-assembly theory was published in IRE Transactions on Information Theory IT-2 (1956), pp. 80-93.
Minsky later said Solomonoff's symbolic ideas led him to switch from working on neural nets to symbolic AI.

Simon and Newell (Operations Research 6(1), 1958, from Simon's 1957 ORSA address) predicted a digital computer would be world chess champion within ten years; Deep Blue beat Kasparov in 1997, 29 years after that 1968 deadline.
Herbert Simon wrote in The New Science of Management Decision (1960, p. 38) that machines would be capable within twenty years of doing any work a man can do; it is often misdated to 1965.
Minsky wrote in Computation: Finite and Infinite Machines (1967, p. 2) that within a generation the problems of creating artificial intelligence would be substantially solved.

Lettvin, Maturana, McCulloch and Pitts's 'What the Frog's Eye Tells the Frog's Brain' (Proc. IRE 1959) found rich feature detection in the retina; Lettvin recalled it disappointed Pitts about logic as the brain's language.
Pitts burned his dissertation and notes and died alone in a Cambridge boarding house on 14 May 1969; McCulloch died four months later, on 24 September 1969.
Around 1952 Wiener abruptly cut off McCulloch, Pitts and Lettvin; according to Wiener's biographers, the cause was a story told by Margaret Wiener. This rests on one family-testimony account.
At AI@50 (Dartmouth, 13-15 July 2006) five original attendees were present: Minsky, Solomonoff, Selfridge, More and McCarthy.

The Office of Naval Research funded Frank Rosenblatt's perceptron program at the Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory, Buffalo, from July 1957 (Project PARA, contract Nonr-2381(00)), and the Ithaca program from September 1959.

On 7 July 1958 the Navy demonstrated in Washington a perceptron simulated on the Weather Bureau's IBM 704 that, after 50 trials, learned to tell punch cards marked on the left from cards marked on the right.

The New York Times (8 July 1958, p. 25) printed the UPI story headlined 'NEW NAVY DEVICE LEARNS BY DOING', whose lede says the Navy expects the computer to 'walk, talk, see, write, reproduce itself and be conscious of its existence'.

Responsibility for the 1958 hype is shared: the lede attributes the prediction to the Navy, but secondary transcriptions of the same story attribute similar sweeping claims to Rosenblatt, and he wrote in summer 1958 'we are about to witness the birth of such a machine'.
Rosenblatt's 'The perceptron: a probabilistic model for information storage and organization in the brain' appeared in Psychological Review 65(6):386-408 in November 1958.

The New Yorker (6 December 1958) said in its own voice that the perceptron struck it as 'the first serious rival to the human brain ever devised', and noted the first perceptron 'has yet to be built' but had been simulated on a 704.

The 'Mechanisation of Thought Processes' symposium at the National Physical Laboratory, Teddington (24-27 November 1958) heard Selfridge's Pandemonium and McCarthy's Advice Taker; Rosenblatt's 'Two Theorems of Statistical Separability in the Perceptron' is in the proceedings.
The Mark I Perceptron was built at CAL Buffalo in 1958-59 (Smithsonian: 'date made 1958'; Jensen & Dunning 2026: assembled June to 14 December 1959) and first demonstrated publicly on 23 June 1960.

Rosenblatt wrote that the Mark I had eight binary response units and 512 association units, used motor-driven potentiometers as integrators and a large patch-panel for connections; its standard retina was a 20x20 array of 400 sensory points.
The Mark I's sensory-to-association wiring was set at random on a plugboard from a table of random numbers and was not learned; only association-to-response weights learned.

Rosenblatt reported the Mark I learned the alphabet in fixed position but that attempts to teach it all 26 letters in two typefaces simultaneously were unsuccessful, 'about the limit of the capacity of the Mark I system'.
From 1963 to 1966 the Mark I was part of a formerly secret NPIC (CIA) effort to develop the perceptron into a tool for photo-interpreters (O'Connor 2022).
The Mark I came to the Smithsonian in 1967 from Cornell as a transfer from ONR (NMAH ID 1987.0819.01) and is currently not on view.

Rosenblatt signed the preface of Principles of Neurodynamics on 15 March 1961 (Spartan Books edition 1962); it blamed the 1958 popular press and called the perceptron 'first and foremost a brain model'.
Rosenblatt cited the Tulsa (Oklahoma) Times headline 'Frankenstein Monster Designed by Navy—Robot That Thinks' as an example of the press coverage.
A figure in Neurodynamics (1961/62) is captioned 'BACK-PROPAGATING ERROR-CORRECTION EXPERIMENTS', a non-gradient procedure that shares only its name with 1986 backpropagation.

The perceptron convergence theorem guarantees error-correction finds a solution in finitely many corrections only if a separating solution exists; Rosenblatt's first proof was not rigorous, rigorous forms are credited to Block, Joseph, Kesten and others, and Block (1962) and Novikoff (1962, mistake bound (R/gamma)^2) published proofs.
In Neurodynamics Rosenblatt wrote that there were 'several logical errors in Papert's argument', an early skirmish with the future co-author of Perceptrons.

In 'Steps Toward Artificial Intelligence' (Proc. IRE, January 1961) Minsky wrote that randomly connected nets could probably never recognise 'the class of figures having two separated parts', and found 'nothing resembling an analysis' in Rosenblatt's reports; Rosenblatt called the article the views of 'the loyal opposition'.
Rosenblatt and Minsky both attended the Bronx High School of Science in the 1940s; sources disagree on which was ahead.

Oliver Selfridge's Pandemonium (presented 1958, published 1959) was a hierarchy of 'demons' in which each cognitive demon 'computes a shriek' and a decision demon selects the loudest; its task was translating hand-keyed Morse code.

Bernard Widrow and Ted Hoff derived the LMS rule on a Friday afternoon in fall 1959 at Stanford, had it running on an analog computer within half an hour, and built the ADALINE neuron by late Sunday afternoon from parts bought at Zack Electronics.
ADALINE took inputs from a 4x4 array of switches (+1/-1), with analog weight knobs and a meter; LMS updates weights from the error before the threshold, a gradient-descent step on squared error.
Widrow attended the 1956 Dartmouth meeting for a week and later wrote he was 'so taken' by the idea of building an artificial brain that he 'never got over it'.
MADALINE (1962) fed many ADALINEs into a fixed logic unit; Madaline Rule I is credited to 'Widrow and his students', with adaptive first layers and a fixed output layer.
Bernard Widrow died on 30 September 2025, aged 95.
Ted Hoff, Widrow's first Stanford doctoral student and LMS co-inventor, later co-invented the Intel 4004 microprocessor.
MIT's Project MAC started 1 July 1963 with $2,220,000 awarded by ONR on behalf of ARPA; about a third of its resources went to Minsky's AI group, most to time-sharing.

By about 1965-66, SRI's group and Widrow's group had largely left neural nets (Widrow for adaptive antennas and signal processing); Nilsson later wrote that what stymied everyone was how to change weights in more than one layer.
Tobermory, a speech-oriented perceptron with about 12,000 weights in magnetic cores, was built at Cornell 1961-1967; by completion digital simulation had overtaken it.
Students lived at Rosenblatt's Brooktondale house near Ithaca and helped build an astronomical observatory there; he also pursued music and mountaineering and campaigned for Eugene McCarthy in 1968.

The ALPAC report (November 1966; committee chaired by John R. Pierce, formed April 1964) found 'no immediate or predictable prospect of useful machine translation'; it put US spending at about $20 million over ten years, a figure Hutchins argues overstates research funding (nearer $12-13 million).
Hutchins says ALPAC's effect was to end substantial US funding of machine translation research for some twenty years; ALPAC concerned machine translation, not neural nets.

Minsky and Papert's Perceptrons (MIT Press, 1969) proved that order-limited single-layer perceptrons cannot compute parity (which needs a detector seeing every point) or connectedness (order growing at least as the square root of retina size).

Perceptrons' final chapter (pp. 231-232) offered only an 'intuitive judgment that the extension is sterile' for multilayer machines, explicitly calling it an important research problem; it proved nothing about trainable hidden layers.

Multilayer threshold networks were already known to compute XOR (McCulloch and Pitts had shown threshold networks compute any Boolean function); the open problem in 1969 was training hidden-unit weights automatically.

Not all multilayer learning was absent in 1969: Amari's 1967 theory of adaptive pattern classifiers derived stochastic-gradient learning (with Saito's experiments on a five-layer net with two modifiable layers), and Ivakhnenko's GMDH grew deep polynomial nets layer by layer; both were little known in the US mainstream.
Minsky received the 1969 ACM Turing Award.

The Mansfield Amendment (Sec. 203, P.L. 91-121, 19 November 1969) barred Defense Department funding of research without 'a direct and apparent relationship to a specific military function or operation'; on 7 October 1970 (P.L. 91-441, Sec. 204) it was softened to a 'potential relationship' test.
ARPA was renamed DARPA in March 1972.
Frank Rosenblatt drowned while sailing the sloop Shearwater on Chesapeake Bay on 11 July 1971, his 43rd birthday.
The second printing of Perceptrons (1972), with the authors' handwritten alterations, carries the handwritten dedication 'In memory of Frank Rosenblatt'; a 1969 dedication is unconfirmed.

Sir James Lighthill's 'Artificial Intelligence: A General Survey' (dated July 1972, published 1973 by the UK Science Research Council) divided AI into categories A, B and C, condemned B (general-purpose 'Building Robots') and blamed disappointment on the combinatorial explosion.
Lighthill's category C explicitly approved computer-based models of neural nets for neurobiology; his target was general-purpose AI and robotics, not neural nets.

Lighthill defended his report in a televised Royal Institution debate in 1973 against Donald Michie, John McCarthy and Richard Gregory (then at Bristol); the exact date is disputed (9 May, June, or filming 4 July with broadcast 30 August).
After the Lighthill report UK academic confidence and funding for AI fell for almost a decade, until the 1982 IKBS review that led to the Alvey programme.
In 1973, aged 49, Lighthill became the first person to swim around the island of Sark; he died in the sea off Sark on 17 July 1998 on his seventh circumnavigation.
DARPA's Speech Understanding Research program (1971) ended in 1976 without its planned follow-on, part of a mid-1970s DARPA turn to applied deliverables.

Seppo Linnainmaa's 1970 University of Helsinki master's thesis described reverse-mode automatic differentiation with FORTRAN code, unrelated to neural nets; the journal version is BIT 16(2):146-160 (1976).

Paul Werbos's August 1974 Harvard thesis 'Beyond Regression' applied reverse-mode derivatives; whether it applied them to neural nets is disputed (Schmidhuber: only 'preliminary, NN-specific discussion', first NN application in Werbos 1982).
Teuvo Kohonen (Helsinki University of Technology) published correlation-matrix memories (1972) and self-organising maps (1982).
Stephen Grossberg developed shunting networks (1973) and Adaptive Resonance Theory (1976).

Kunihiko Fukushima's Neocognitron (NHK Broadcasting Science Research Laboratories, Tokyo; Biological Cybernetics 36:193-202, received 28 October 1979, published 1980) alternated S-cell and C-cell layers and is a direct ancestor of convolutional networks.

In 'One AI or Many?' (Daedalus, Winter 1988) Papert retold the connectionists' 'Snow White' version of events, conceded 'some hostility in the energy behind the research' partly over funding, but said most of the motivation came from more fundamental concerns.

Whether Perceptrons 'killed' neural-net research is contested: the PDP group and popular histories say yes; Olazaran (1996) argues the 'official history' reflected the institutional legitimation of symbolic AI, and Baldi (2022) calls the story an exaggeration propagated by the PDP group.
H. D. Block's 1970 review said Perceptrons studied 'a severely limited class of machines from a viewpoint quite alien to Rosenblatt's' and called the title 'seriously misleading'.
DoD funding for mathematics and computer science reached a 20-year low in 1975 (NRC, as cited by AI Now); George Heilmeier was DARPA director 1975-77.
The 'first winter' was not uniform: DARPA AI money to MIT, Stanford and CMU continued with more strings attached; neural nets, machine translation and UK AI were hit hardest, at different times.

John Hopfield's 'Neural networks and physical systems with emergent collective computational abilities' (PNAS 79(8):2554-2558, April 1982) showed a symmetric network of binary units has an energy that only decreases, giving a content-addressable memory.

As a National Academy member Hopfield published in PNAS without review under a five-page limit; it was the first paper in which he used the word 'neuron', and he said it gave many physicists an entryway to neuroscience.
Hopfield first presented his network in summer 1981 at a symposium in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles and said he had never met anyone who remembered hearing the talk.
Hopfield moved from Princeton to Caltech in February 1980 and kept a part-time Bell Labs affiliation; he tried out models on Caltech's quantum-chemistry computing facility.

Ackley, Hinton and Sejnowski's 'A Learning Algorithm for Boltzmann Machines' (Cognitive Science 9(1):147-169, 1985) used stochastic units, simulated annealing and a local rule comparing clamped and free-running co-activation statistics.

In 250 tests of the 4-2-4 encoder the Boltzmann machine always found a global minimum, with a median of 110 learning cycles and a longest of 1,810; severe simulation speed limits kept experiments small.
Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams's 'Learning representations by back-propagating errors' appeared in Nature 323:533-536 on 9 October 1986 (received 1 May, accepted 31 July 1986).
In the 1986 paper a 6-input, 2-hidden-unit network learned mirror-symmetry detection in 1,425 sweeps through all 64 input vectors (learning rate 0.1, momentum 0.9).

In the 1986 family-trees task (two isomorphic English and Italian families, 104 triples, 100 used for training), hidden units came to encode nationality, generation and family branch, and the network generalised correctly to the four held-out triples.
The 1986 paper itself said the procedure 'in its current form, is not a plausible model of learning in brains', and reported the network 'very rarely gets stuck in poor local minima'.
The 1986 Nature paper acknowledged independent discovery by David Parker and Yann Le Cun but did not cite Linnainmaa or Werbos.
The 1986 Nature paper acknowledges funding from the System Development Foundation and the Office of Naval Research, and prints CMU's address as 'Pittsburgh, Philadelphia 15213'.

Backpropagation was invented several times independently: control-theory precursors (Kelley 1960, Bryson 1961, Dreyfus 1962), Linnainmaa 1970, Werbos 1974/1982, Parker 1985, LeCun 1985 and Rumelhart (1982 re-derivation); the 1986 paper popularised it. Credit remains disputed.
In April 2020 Hinton wrote that he had never claimed to have invented backpropagation and that what he claimed was to have clearly demonstrated it could learn interesting internal representations.

Per his own CV, Hinton was at Sussex (1976-78), UCSD (1978-80), the MRC Applied Psychology Unit Cambridge (1980-82), UCSD again (Jan-June 1982), Carnegie Mellon (Oct 1982-June 1987) and the University of Toronto from July 1987, when he became a CIFAR Fellow.
Hinton left the US partly because most American AI funding came from the Department of Defense and partly from disillusionment with Reagan-era politics.

In 1987 Hinton joined CIFAR's existing Artificial Intelligence, Robotics & Society programme (founded 1983); CIFAR describes the neural-network field at the time as met with widespread skepticism and an episodic dearth of funding.

The two Parallel Distributed Processing volumes (Rumelhart, McClelland and the PDP Research Group, MIT Press, 1986; 1,158 pages) sold out a 6,000-copy first run before going to press, with about 30,000 in print two years later.
The share of connectionist talks at the Cognitive Science Society meeting rose from 17% (1984) to 23% (1985) to 31% (1986).

NETtalk (Sejnowski and Rosenberg, Complex Systems 1, 1987) mapped a 7-letter window (203 input units) through 80 hidden units to 26 outputs with 18,629 weights, voiced through a DECtalk synthesiser; trained on 1,024 words from a first-grader's transcript it went from babble to understandable text by 10 passes and reached 95% phoneme accuracy after 50.

Pomerleau's ALVINN (NIPS 1988, published 1989) was a backprop network with a 30x32 blue-channel video retina, an 8x32 range-finder retina, 29 hidden units and 46 outputs, trained on 1,200 simulated road images; it drove CMU's NAVLAB van at 0.5 m/s along a 400 m wooded campus path.
The 1995 'No Hands Across America' drive (23-31 July 1995), in which CMU's Navlab 5 steered 2,797 of 2,849 miles (98.2%), used the RALPH system, not ALVINN.

In 1989 Cybenko, Hornik-Stinchcombe-White and Funahashi independently proved that one hidden layer suffices in principle to approximate continuous functions; these are existence results saying nothing about training, data or size.
Fodor and Pylyshyn ('Connectionism and cognitive architecture', Cognition 28:3-71, 1988) argued connectionist networks lack systematicity and are at best implementations of classical architectures.

Pinker and Prince ('On language and connectionism', Cognition 28:73-193, 1988) argued the Rumelhart-McClelland past-tense model fails empirically and that connectionists' claims about the dispensability of rules must be rejected.

Lake and Baroni (Nature 623:115-121, online 25 October 2023) wrote that the systematicity challenge 'persists' and claimed in the next sentence to have addressed it with meta-learning; critics dispute whether it is solved.
Terry Sejnowski was Hopfield's PhD student (Princeton, 1978); he moved to the Salk Institute in the late 1980s (1988 per Salk, 1989 per his own Brain Prize biography).

On 8 October 2024 the Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton 'for foundational discoveries and inventions that enable machine learning with artificial neural networks'.
David Rumelhart died on 13 March 2011, aged 68, of complications of a progressive neurodegenerative disease (the New York Times names Pick's disease, citing his son).

The Rumelhart-McClelland past-tense model (PDP vol. 2, ch. 18) used Wickelfeature encodings and a single layer of modifiable connections, trained first on 10 high-frequency verbs then on 420 verbs presented 190 times.
Edward Feigenbaum drew from DENDRAL (begun at Stanford in 1965) the 'knowledge-is-power hypothesis (later called the Knowledge Principle)': domain knowledge matters more than the reasoning method.

In a blinded evaluation (Yu et al., JAMA 242(12), 21 September 1979) of ten meningitis cases, eight outside infectious-disease experts rated 65% of MYCIN's prescriptions acceptable versus a mean of 55.5% (range 42.5-62.5%) for five Stanford faculty specialists.
MYCIN, written in Lisp and run on a DEC PDP-10 over the ARPANET, was never put into routine clinical use.

John McDermott's R1/XCON was begun in December 1978 in OPS4, used by DEC from January 1980, rewritten in OPS5 from April 1980 (500 rules), and grew to about 3,300 rules by November 1983 and 6,200 by 1987, with about half its rules changing each year.
XCON's savings for DEC are variously quoted ($15M, $25M a year, $40M over six years); 'tens of millions of dollars' is safe.

Japan's MITI launched the Fifth Generation Computer Systems project at ICOT in Tokyo in April 1982 under Kazuhiro Fuchi, aiming at parallel logic-programming 'knowledge information processing' machines; it spent about ¥54 billion over the main project, 1982-1992 (a follow-on ran to 1994).
ICOT built five models of Parallel Inference Machine; PIM/p had 512 processors and PIM/m 256, both preserved at the National Museum of Nature and Science, Tokyo.
Feigenbaum and McCorduck's 1983 book The Fifth Generation framed the Japanese project as 'Japan's Computer Challenge to the World'.
MCC, a US industry research consortium under Admiral Bobby Ray Inman, was founded in late 1982 and sited in Austin, Texas in 1983; it ceased operations in 2000.

DARPA's Strategic Computing Initiative (announced 1983, about $1 billion over 1983-1993) had three flagship applications: an Autonomous Land Vehicle, a Pilot's Associate and a naval Battle Management system.

The UK government accepted the Alvey Programme in April 1983 (up to £200 million from government plus £150 million from industry), with intelligent knowledge-based systems as one of four strands; its director took up his post on 1 June 1983.
Doug Lenat began Cyc at MCC in July 1984 to hand-encode common sense 'over the coming decade', estimating about 150 man-years of data entry; it spun out as Cycorp in January 1995.
Lenat, Prakash and Shepherd wrote in 1985 that simply having an online encyclopedia would be of little use because current AI could draw practically nothing from raw text.
Doug Lenat died in Austin on 31 August 2023, aged 72.

At AAAI-84 in Austin (August 1984) Drew McDermott chaired the panel 'The Dark Ages of AI' with Waldrop, Schank, Chandrasekaran and John McDermott, sketching a worst case he said was 'called the AI Winter by some'; Minsky was not on the published panel.
symbolics.com, registered 15 March 1985 by the Lisp-machine maker Symbolics (incorporated 9 April 1980), was the first .com domain name.

Around 1987 the dedicated Lisp-machine market collapsed as Sun workstations and PCs running Lisp overtook it; LMI went bankrupt in 1987. Historian Daniel Crevier wrote that an industry worth half a billion dollars was replaced in a single year.
Jack Schwartz took over DARPA's ISTO (IPTO's successor) in 1986 or 1987 and, per McCorduck, cut AI funding 'deeply and brutally'.
DARPA ran a Neural Network Study from October 1987 to February 1988, directed by Bernard Widrow.

The Fifth Generation project's main phase ended with the FGCS'92 conference in Tokyo in June 1992; the New York Times headline (5 June 1992) called it 'Japan's Lost Generation', while ICOT defended it as basic research.
The Fifth Generation project was about logic programming and parallel inference (Prolog/KL1), not neural networks.

Rodney Brooks's 'Elephants Don't Play Chess' (1990) argued 'the world is its own best model'; 'Intelligence without representation' (received September 1987, published 1991) called representation 'the wrong unit of abstraction' for the bulkiest parts of intelligent systems.
Brooks's robot Herbert used 24 slow 8-bit processors and was programmed to wander offices and steal empty soda cans; Genghis was a 1 kg six-legged walker.

Hubert Dreyfus argued in What Computers Can't Do (1972) that expertise is intuitive and embodied; in the 1992 MIT Press edition he called GOFAI a 'degenerating research program'. John McCarthy rejected the charge in 1996.

Sepp Hochreiter's 1991 TU Munich diploma thesis (in German) and Bengio, Simard and Frasconi (IEEE Trans. Neural Networks 5(2), March 1994) independently showed that error signals vanish or explode as they are propagated back through many layers or time steps.

Joseph Weizenbaum's NYRB review of The Fifth Generation (27 October 1983) called Simon and Newell's 1958 ambition 'as absurd today as it was twenty-five years ago', tying it to Fifth Generation claims.
Whether expert systems failed is contested: the commercial bubble burst, but XCON ran for over a decade and rule engines survived inside ordinary business software without the 'AI' label.

LeCun et al. (AT&T Bell Labs, Holmdel; Neural Computation 1(4):541-551, 1989) trained a backprop network on 9,298 handwritten ZIP-code digits from Buffalo, NY mail (7,291 train, 2,007 test), reaching 5.0% raw test error.
Yann LeCun joined Larry Jackel's Adaptive Systems Research Department at AT&T Bell Labs, Holmdel, in 1988.

LeCun, Bottou, Bengio and Haffner's 'Gradient-Based Learning Applied to Document Recognition' (Proc. IEEE 86(11), November 1998) introduced LeNet-5 and the MNIST benchmark (60,000 train, 10,000 test); LeNet-5 had 0.95% error without distortions.
MNIST mixes NIST Special Database 3 (written by Census Bureau employees) and Special Database 1 (written by high-school students).
A Bell Labs convolutional check reader, fielded in US banks since June 1996, was 'deployed commercially and reads several million checks per day'; LeCun estimates it read about 10% of US checks.

Support vector machines: Boser, Guyon and Vapnik brought the kernel trick to maximum-margin classifiers at COLT 1992; Cortes and Vapnik's soft-margin 'Support-Vector Networks' appeared in Machine Learning 20(3):273-297 in September 1995.
Vladimir Vapnik developed VC theory at Moscow's Institute of Control Sciences and moved to AT&T Bell Labs, Holmdel, at the end of 1990.

On 14 March 1995 at Bell Labs, Larry Jackel bet one fancy dinner that by 14 March 2000 people would understand quantitatively why big neural nets work, and Vapnik bet that by 14 March 2005 no one in his right mind would use neural nets essentially like those of 1995; LeCun signed as witness. Each man lost one bet.
Freund and Schapire's AdaBoost (EuroCOLT 1995; JCSS 55(1), August 1997) combined weak learners with provable guarantees and won the 2003 Gödel Prize.
Leo Breiman's 'Random Forests' (Machine Learning 45:5-32, October 2001) combined bootstrap-sampled decision trees with random feature selection.

Breiman's 'Statistical Modeling: The Two Cultures' (Statistical Science 16(3), August 2001) estimated 98% of statisticians in the data-modelling culture, said SVMs had proved more accurate than neural nets, and conceded a hand-crafted neural net beat his random forest on ZIP codes (5.1% vs 6.2%).

Judea Pearl coined 'Bayesian network' in 1985 and consolidated the field in Probabilistic Reasoning in Intelligent Systems (1988); he received the 2011 ACM Turing Award for a calculus for probabilistic and causal reasoning.
Frederick Jelinek's IBM group pioneered statistical speech recognition and, from 1987, statistical machine translation trained on Canadian parliamentary Hansards (Brown et al. 1990, 1993).

Jelinek's 'fire a linguist' quip exists in many versions; his own 2004 recollection dates it to a December 1988 workshop in Wayne, Pennsylvania, but it is absent from the 1988 proceedings and a variant is dated 1985.

Hochreiter and Schmidhuber's 'Long Short-Term Memory' (Neural Computation 9(8):1735-1780, November 1997) used constant error carousels with gates to bridge time lags over 1,000 steps; the forget gate was added in 2000 by Gers, Schmidhuber and Cummins.

Bengio, Ducharme, Vincent and Jauvin's neural probabilistic language model (NIPS 2000; JMLR 3:1137-1155, 2003) learned a distributed vector per word and beat the best n-gram models (Brown: 252 vs 312 perplexity; AP News: 109 vs 117); the AP run took about three weeks on 40 CPUs.

IBM's Deep Blue beat Garry Kasparov 3.5-2.5 at the Equitable Center, New York, winning Game 6 in 19 moves on 11 May 1997; it used about 30 processors plus 480 custom chess chips searching 200 million positions per second, and no neural-net learning.
Deep Blue's evaluation function was hand-designed but its parameter values were 'determined by analyzing thousands of master games'.
Kasparov suspected human help in Game 2 of the 1997 match; IBM said human intervention was only between games, as the rules allowed. No evidence of cheating exists.
In 2004 CIFAR launched Neural Computation and Adaptive Perception (NCAP), proposed by Hinton with Bengio, David Fleet and others; per CIFAR's biography Hinton directed it from 2004 to 2013.
LeCun told the Toronto Star (17 April 2015) that his group was 'outcast a little bit' and 'couldn't get our papers published'; Bengio said 2004 'was the worst possible time'.

LeCun (IEEE Spectrum, 18 February 2015) dated a 'Neural Net Winter' to the late 1990s and early 2000s and blamed the attitude that 'you had to have ironclad theory'; he called himself, Hinton and Bengio 'the so-called Deep Learning conspiracy'.

In June 2015 Schmidhuber published a critique of the 'Deep Learning Conspiracy' Nature review for under-crediting earlier pioneers; he notes 'deep learning' as a term predates them (Dechter 1986; Aizenberg et al. 2000).

In 2012 CVPR rejected Farabet, Couprie, Najman and LeCun's convnet scene-parsing paper, which went to ICML 2012; whether this shows bias is contested since two deep-learning face papers were accepted at CVPR 2012.

The Netflix Prize (launched 2 October 2006, $1 million for 10% over Cinematch, 100,480,507 ratings) ended in a tie at 10.06%; BellKor's Pragmatic Chaos won by submitting about 20 minutes earlier (winner named 18 September 2009) with a blend of many models.
Viola and Jones's boosted cascade (CVPR 2001) showed boosting-based object detection running in real time.
In LeCun et al. 1998's MNIST comparison: linear classifier 12.0%, Gaussian SVM 1.4%, LeNet-5 0.95%, virtual SVM with distortions 0.8%, boosted LeNet-4 0.7%.

Hinton, Osindero and Teh's 'A fast learning algorithm for deep belief nets' (Neural Computation 18(7):1527-1554, July 2006) trained a deep network one layer at a time as stacked RBMs (labels entering only at the top), reaching 1.25% MNIST error versus 1.4% for SVMs and 1.5% for backprop; greedy training took a few hours per layer in Matlab on a 3 GHz Xeon, about a week in total.
A footnote to the 2006 DBN paper says the network was left running with a very small learning rate and after six weeks the test error was fluctuating between 1.12% and 1.31%.

Hinton and Salakhutdinov's 'Reducing the Dimensionality of Data with Neural Networks' (Science 313:504-507, 28 July 2006) used layer-wise pretraining to initialise deep autoencoders (e.g. 784-1000-500-250-30 for digits) that compressed data far better than PCA, and declared 'All three conditions are now satisfied'.

Bengio, Lamblin, Popovici and Larochelle (NIPS 2006, 'Greedy Layer-Wise Training of Deep Networks') and Ranzato, Poultney, Chopra and LeCun (sparse energy-based models, 0.39% MNIST) generalised the pretraining recipe.
Hinton, LeCun and Bengio wrote in Nature (2015) that interest in deep feedforward networks was revived around 2006 by a group brought together by CIFAR.

NVIDIA launched the GeForce 8800 GTX (G80), the first CUDA-capable GPU, on 8 November 2006; the CUDA SDK went to beta in February 2007. CUDA was a general-purpose GPU platform, not created for deep learning.

Raina, Madhavan and Ng (ICML 2009) trained deep belief nets on a GeForce GTX 280 up to 70 times faster than a dual-core CPU, cutting a four-layer, 100-million-parameter model from several weeks to about a day.

Cireșan, Meier, Gambardella and Schmidhuber (IDSIA, arXiv 1 March 2010) reached a record 0.35% MNIST error with 'good old on-line back-propagation' on plain deep MLPs, deformed images and a GTX 280 GPU, with no pretraining.
At IJCNN 2011 an IDSIA committee of GPU CNNs scored 99.46% on the German Traffic Sign Recognition Benchmark, against 98.84% for the average human and 99.22% for the best individual human.

Schmidhuber argues IDSIA's GPU CNN ('DanNet') won four image-recognition contests before AlexNet and triggered the CNN revolution; the mainstream dates vision's turn to ImageNet 2012. Both the IDSIA wins and AlexNet's decisive role are documented.

Fei-Fei Li arrived at Princeton in January 2007; her office neighbour was Christiane Fellbaum of WordNet (begun 1985 by George A. Miller, over 145,000 words), whose noun hierarchy became ImageNet's skeleton. Li launched ImageNet with Kai Li (no relation).

Li's 2010 slides estimated hand-labelling ImageNet would take about 19 years ('no graduate students would want to do this project!'); after 'discovering crowdsourcing' in summer 2008, the dataset went from 0 images (July 2008) to 11 million images in 15,000+ categories (April 2010).
Over the whole project, almost 50,000 Amazon Mechanical Turk workers from 167 countries cleaned and labelled nearly a billion candidate images (Li, TED 2015).

The CVPR 2009 ImageNet paper (Deng, Dong, Socher, Li, Li and Fei-Fei) reported 3.2 million images in 5,247 synsets across 12 subtrees; the full dataset later reached about 14 million images in 21,841 synsets.

Li said colleagues advised her to 'do something more useful for my tenure' and that funding was a constant struggle; Olga Russakovsky recalled that prestige came from building models and most people wondered why collecting a dataset would be intellectually interesting.

ILSVRC began in 2010 as a 'taster competition' alongside PASCAL VOC with 1,000 categories and 1.2 million training images; 35 submissions from 11 teams were presented on 11 September 2010 at ECCV in Crete, won by NEC-UIUC (28.2% top-5) with hand-designed features and SVMs. XRCE won 2011 at about 25.8%.

Mohamed, Dahl and Hinton (NIPS 2009 speech workshop) reached 23.0% phone error on TIMIT with a pretrained deep net (four hidden layers of 2,048 units plus a 128-unit bottleneck) on an NVIDIA Tesla S1070 GPU, against a previous best of 24.4%.
Hinton recalled (to VentureBeat in 2022) telling about 1,000 researchers at NIPS 2009 that they should all buy GPUs.

Toronto student George Dahl interned at Microsoft Research from June 2010; context-dependent DNN-HMMs tested on Bing voice-search data cut sentence error by about 16% relative, and Seide, Li and Yu (2011) cut Switchboard word error from 27.4% to 18.5%.
Microsoft's first product with DNN speech recognition, announced 14 June 2012, was the MAVIS audio-video indexing service (10-20% relative error reduction), not Bing voice search on phones.

Android 4.1 Jelly Bean (released to manufacturing 9 July 2012) shipped a DNN acoustic model for voice search; Google wrote on 6 August 2012 that when you speak to your Android phone you are probably talking to a neural network. This was about three months before AlexNet's ImageNet result.
In November 2012 Toronto, Microsoft Research, Google and IBM published a joint review of deep neural networks for acoustic modelling in IEEE Signal Processing Magazine 29(6).

Nair and Hinton introduced rectified linear units for RBMs at ICML 2010; Glorot, Bordes and Bengio (AISTATS 2011) showed deep rectifier nets need no unsupervised pretraining on large labelled datasets.

The dropout paper (Hinton, Srivastava, Krizhevsky, Sutskever and Salakhutdinov, arXiv 1207.0580, 3 July 2012) reduced overfitting by randomly omitting half of the feature detectors on each training case.

Google Brain's 'cat' paper (Le et al., ICML 2012) trained a nine-layer locally connected sparse autoencoder with 1 billion connections on one frame from each of 10 million YouTube videos, using 1,000 machines (16,000 CPU cores) for three days; a neuron became a face detector without labels.
The cat paper's 15.8% accuracy on 22,000-category ImageNet required supervised training on labelled ImageNet on top of the unsupervised features (13.6% without the pretraining).
The New York Times (John Markoff, 26 June 2012, p. B1) ran 'How Many Computers to Identify a Cat? 16,000', quoting Jeff Dean that the network 'basically invented the concept of a cat'.
Google Brain began in 2011 inside Google X, founded by Jeff Dean, Greg Corrado and Andrew Ng.
In 2013 Coates, Catanzaro, Ng and colleagues trained 1-billion-parameter networks on just three GPU machines in a couple of days.

From about 2006 to 2010-2011 the working belief was that deep nets need unsupervised layer-wise pretraining; it eroded gradually (Cireșan 2010, Martens 2010, Glorot 2010-2011, AlexNet 2012), and in 2015 the pioneers wrote it 'was only needed for small data sets'. The exact end date is interpretive.

Hinton's 2019 slides recount NIPS rejecting a 2007 deep-learning paper because it had already accepted one on the same topic, a ~2009 ICML reviewer saying neural-net papers had no place in ICML, and a ~2010 CVPR reviewer rejecting a LeCun paper because 'everything is learned'.
Amazon Mechanical Turk, the platform on which ImageNet was labelled, permanently closed on 30 September 2026.

At ILSVRC-2012 the University of Toronto's SuperVision team (Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, Geoffrey Hinton) achieved 15.3% top-5 error (0.15315); the runner-up, the University of Tokyo's ISI team using Fisher Vectors, scored 26.2%.

AlexNet's 15.3% was an ensemble of seven nets, two of them pre-trained on the ~15-million-image Fall 2011 ImageNet release; the best entry without extra data was 16.4%, and a single CNN scored 18.2% on validation.
The ILSVRC-2012 submission deadline was 30 September 2012 (extended on 17 September); preliminary results went out 8 October, the workshop was 12 October and full results 13 October.
AlexNet was first presented on 12 October 2012 at the ILSVRC workshop of ECCV in Florence; Krizhevsky gave the last talk of the session (17:05-17:30).
Hinton did not attend Florence because of a chronic back problem (he could not sit, so did not fly); by Li's account the room was so crowded LeCun stood against the back wall.
Cade Metz reports that by December 2012 Hinton had not taken a seat for seven years because of his back, and travelled to Lake Tahoe lying down on a bus, a train and a taxi.
AlexNet had five convolutional and three fully connected layers, about 60 million parameters and 650,000 neurons, and was trained on about 1.2 million labelled images in 1,000 classes.
AlexNet trained for five to six days (about 90 epochs) on two NVIDIA GeForce GTX 580 3 GB consumer graphics cards (the GTX 580 launched 9 November 2010).

The Computer History Museum says AlexNet trained on a computer with two NVIDIA cards in Krizhevsky's bedroom at his parents' house; NVIDIA's 2023 blog says a University of Toronto lab. The CHM account is preferred.

Per the CHM, Sutskever believed neural-network performance would scale with data and in 2011 convinced Krizhevsky to train a CNN on ImageNet, with Hinton as principal investigator; Krizhevsky wrote the cuda-convnet GPU code.

AlexNet's paper credits ReLU (a four-layer CNN reached 25% CIFAR-10 training error six times faster than tanh), two-GPU training, local response normalisation, overlapping pooling, data augmentation (crops, mirrors, PCA colour jitter) and dropout (p = 0.5 in fc6 and fc7).

AlexNet's two GPUs communicated only at certain layers (into conv3 and the fully connected layers); without being told to, the first-layer filters on one GPU came out largely colour-agnostic and on the other largely colour-specific, in every run.

By derived count, about 96% of AlexNet's parameters sit in its three fully connected layers (fc6 alone about 62%), while about 92% of its roughly 0.72 billion multiply-adds per image are in the convolutional layers.

AlexNet's paper gives a 224-pixel input; the original 2012 cuda-convnet code rounds conv output size up, so 224 with no padding gives the stated 55; some re-implementations (Caffe) use 227, torchvision uses 224 with padding 2.
The AlexNet paper said its results 'can be improved simply by waiting for faster GPUs and bigger datasets to become available', and that it used no unsupervised pre-training.

Per Cade Metz, during NIPS 2012 at Harrah's, Lake Tahoe, Hinton auctioned the three-person company DNNresearch by email from Room 731 among Baidu, Google, Microsoft and DeepMind; he stopped at $44 million and chose Google. The acquisition was announced in March 2013 without disclosed terms.

Per Metz, DeepMind bid in company shares and dropped out early; Microsoft dropped out near $22 million; the laptop sat on an upturned trash can so Hinton could type standing; the Google dinner fell on Hinton's 65th birthday.
ImageNet top-5 error fell from 15.3% (2012) to 11.2% (Clarifai, 2013), 6.7% (GoogLeNet, 2014) and 3.57% (ResNet, Microsoft Research, December 2015, up to 152 layers).
By ILSVRC 2013 all top five classification teams used convolutional nets (second-placed NUS was a hybrid with its traditional PASCAL solution).
GoogLeNet (2014) used 12x fewer parameters than AlexNet and was trained with a CPU-based DistBelief implementation.
Oxford's VGG team, third in 2012 with Fisher vectors, built the 16-19-layer VGG CNNs in 2014; VGG found AlexNet's local response normalisation did not help.

The 5.1% 'human' ImageNet error was Andrej Karpathy alone, on 1,500 test images after training himself; another labeller scored about 12% on 280 images. He later estimated dedicated expert ensembles might reach about 3%.

Claims that machines surpassed humans on ImageNet in 2015 (PReLU 4.94%, batch norm 4.8%, ResNet 3.57%) are contested: the baseline is one person, top-5 scoring is lenient, a fresh test set (ImageNetV2) cut accuracy 11-14 points, and at least 6% of ImageNet validation labels are wrong.

In June 2015 ILSVRC organisers found Baidu's Deep Image team made about 200 test submissions from 30 accounts against a two-per-week limit and barred Baidu for 12 months; Baidu fired team lead Ren Wu, who denied wrongdoing.
On 20 March 2025 the Computer History Museum, with Google, released AlexNet's original 2012 source code under a BSD-2 licence after five years of negotiation.
The CHM states that before AlexNet almost none of the leading computer vision papers used neural nets, and after it almost all would.

AlexNet was not the first GPU CNN (IDSIA's 2011 GPU CNNs won earlier contests, and AlexNet cites Cireșan twice) but was the decisive demonstration on the benchmark that converted computer vision; this is contested in emphasis, not fact.

Before 2012, mainstream computer vision built recognisers from hand-engineered features (SIFT, HOG, LBP), encodings such as Fisher Vectors and linear SVMs; every non-Toronto ILSVRC-2012 entry used such pipelines.

Mikolov, Chen, Corrado and Dean posted word2vec (arXiv 1301.3781) on 16 January 2013: shallow log-linear CBOW and skip-gram models that learned word vectors from 1.6 billion words in under a day; Google open-sourced the toolkit on 14 August 2013.
Mikolov, Yih and Zweig (NAACL 2013) reported that 'King - Man + Woman' results in a vector very close to 'Queen'.

Nissim, van Noord and van der Goot showed the standard analogy code forbids returning input words; allowing them drops accuracy on Google's analogy set from 0.74 to 0.21, mostly because the method returns one of the question's own words.

Bolukbasi et al. (2016) showed Google News word embeddings 'exhibit female/male gender stereotypes to a disturbing extent' ('man is to computer programmer as woman is to homemaker'); Nissim et al. argued some famous biased analogies are artefacts of the constraint, without denying bias.
The 2013 word2vec phrases paper (negative sampling) won the NeurIPS 2023 Test of Time Award.

Sutskever, Vinyals and Le's seq2seq (arXiv 10 September 2014) read a source sentence into one vector with a 4-layer LSTM and decoded French; an ensemble of five reversed-input LSTMs scored 34.81 BLEU versus 33.30 for phrase-based SMT, the best single net 30.59; each model trained about ten days on an 8-GPU machine.
Seq2seq's authors found that reversing the order of source-sentence words improved performance markedly and were 'surprised by the extent of the improvement'.

Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio (arXiv 1 September 2014) called the fixed-length vector 'a bottleneck' and let the decoder soft-search the source sentence at each step, the first widely adopted neural attention; it beat Moses only on sentences without unknown words (36.15 vs 35.63).
Cho et al. (arXiv 3 June 2014) introduced the RNN Encoder-Decoder with the gated recurrent unit.

Google's Neural Machine Translation (GNMT; arXiv 26 September 2016) used 8-layer LSTM encoder and decoder with attention, wordpieces and TPUs, cutting translation errors by about 60% in human side-by-side ratings on isolated simple sentences; Chinese-English moved fully to it (about 18 million translations a day).
The New York Times Magazine (14 December 2016) reported the neural translation system, built in about nine months, made overnight improvements roughly equal to the old system's lifetime gains.
Goodfellow and co-authors posted 'Generative Adversarial Nets' on 10 June 2014: a generator and discriminator in a minimax game, likened to counterfeiters and police.
As MIT Technology Review tells it (2018, reporter's narration), Goodfellow conceived GANs in a Montréal bar, Les 3 Brasseurs, coded the first one that night and it worked the first time.
Schmidhuber argues GANs are special cases of his 1990 artificial curiosity and related to 1991 predictability minimisation; most of the field treats GANs as distinct.
DeepMind was incorporated in London on 23 September 2010 (as 'Friars 2022 Limited', renamed 15 November 2010) by Demis Hassabis, Shane Legg and Mustafa Suleyman.

DeepMind's DQN (arXiv December 2013; Nature 518, February 2015) learned 49 Atari 2600 games from pixels and score with one architecture, beating prior reinforcement learning on 43 and exceeding 75% of a professional tester's score on 29; it discovered Breakout's tunnel strategy but failed at Montezuma's Revenge.
Google acquired DeepMind in January 2014 for a reported £400 million; reports range from about $400 million to $650 million and no figure was officially confirmed.
Yann LeCun announced on 9 December 2013, at NIPS in Lake Tahoe, that he would direct Facebook's new AI research lab.
Andrew Ng joined Baidu in May 2014 to lead its AI research across Silicon Valley and Beijing labs.

OpenAI was announced on 11 December 2015 as a non-profit with Sam Altman and Elon Musk as co-chairs, Ilya Sutskever as research director and Greg Brockman as CTO; funders 'committed $1 billion' while expecting to spend only a tiny fraction in the next few years.
In October 2014 at MIT's AeroAstro Centennial Symposium, Elon Musk called AI probably 'our biggest existential threat' and said 'we are summoning the demon'.

In May 2014 computer-Go pioneer Rémi Coulom guessed a machine would beat a professional without handicap in 'maybe ten years'; the AlphaGo paper called the feat 'previously believed to be at least a decade away'.
In October 2015 AlphaGo beat European champion Fan Hui 5-0 in formal games (3-2 in informal fast games) at DeepMind in London; its distributed version used 1,202 CPUs and 176 GPUs.

AlphaGo combined a policy network and a value network, first trained on 30 million positions from human KGS games then by self-play reinforcement learning, with Monte Carlo tree search; Go has a branching factor of about 250 versus about 35 for chess.
AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol 4-1 at the Four Seasons Hotel, Seoul, 9-15 March 2016, for a $1 million prize; the Lee version ran on 48 TPUs, and DeepMind says over 200 million people watched.

In game 2 (10 March 2016), AlphaGo's move 37 (its 19th stone) was one its policy network estimated a human would play with about a one-in-ten-thousand chance; Lee left the room and took nearly fifteen minutes to respond.

In game 4 (13 March 2016), Lee Sedol's move 78 wedge won humanity's only game against AlphaGo in the match; Hassabis said AlphaGo had also rated it at one in ten thousand. In 2019 Yonhap paraphrased Lee as attributing the win to a bug in AlphaGo.
Fan Hui was ranked 633rd in the world when he lost to AlphaGo and rose into the 300s after months of sparring with it.

AlphaGo Zero (Nature, 19 October 2017), trained with no human games, beat AlphaGo Lee 100-0 after 72 hours of self-play and AlphaGo Master 89-11 after 40 days; it played on one 4-TPU machine but trained on Google Cloud with 64 GPU workers and 19 CPU parameter servers.
Lee Sedol retired in November 2019, telling Yonhap that with AI in Go 'there is an entity that cannot be defeated'.

Szegedy et al. (arXiv 21 December 2013) showed hardly perceptible perturbations make deep networks misclassify images; Goodfellow, Shlens and Szegedy (December 2014) turned a 57.7% 'panda' into a 99.3% 'gibbon' and attributed the effect to excessive linearity.

Gary Marcus's 'Deep Learning: A Critical Appraisal' (arXiv 2 January 2018) listed ten concerns and argued deep learning must be supplemented by other techniques to reach AGI; Marcus and LeCun debated at NYU on 5 October 2017.
Hinton said in September 2017 (as quoted in Marcus 2018) that the future depends on some graduate student deeply suspicious of everything he has said.

Buolamwini and Gebru's Gender Shades (FAT* February 2018) found commercial gender classifiers from Microsoft, Face++ and IBM erred on up to 34.7% of darker-skinned women but at most 0.8% of lighter-skinned men, using a 1,270-person parliamentarian benchmark.

Raji and Buolamwini's follow-up (AIES, January 2019) found all three audited companies released new API versions within seven months, with darker-female error falling by 17.7-30.4 points, while non-audited Amazon and Kairos showed 31.37% and 22.50%.
Joy Buolamwini's TEDxBeaconStreet talk (recorded 19 November 2016) described a face-analysis project that could not detect her face unless she wore a white mask.

On 27 March 2019 ACM named Bengio, Hinton and LeCun recipients of the 2018 A.M. Turing Award 'for conceptual and engineering breakthroughs that have made deep neural networks a critical component of computing' ($1 million, funded by Google); the 'Fathers of the Deep Learning Revolution' framing is contested by those who stress earlier contributors.

MIT Technology Review (31 March 2016) reported Hassabis describing DeepMind's effort as aimed at 'solving intelligence, and then using that to solve everything else'; the popular exact wording 'Solve intelligence...' is untraced.

In 2017 recurrent networks (LSTMs, GRUs) were, in the Transformer paper's own first words, 'firmly established as state of the art approaches in sequence modeling and transduction problems such as language modeling and machine translation', and attention was used 'in conjunction with a recurrent network' in 'all but a few cases'.

Per Wired's oral history, in 2016 Jakob Uszkoreit suggested self-attention to Illia Polosukhin over lunch in a Google cafe for a fast question-answering problem; Uszkoreit, Polosukhin and Ashish Vaswani wrote a design document titled 'Transformers: Iterative Self-Attention and Processing for Various Tasks', which ended with a cartoon of six Transformers zapping lasers in mountainous terrain.

Wired reports the design-doc trio (Uszkoreit, Polosukhin, Vaswani) picked the name 'transformers' from 'day zero' because the mechanism transforms the information it takes in; Uszkoreit's two childhood Transformer toys were an added reason, not the sole one.

Illia Polosukhin, born in Ukraine, left Google in early 2017 before the paper was finished and co-founded NEAR, a blockchain company and the only one of the eight authors' companies not built on transformers.

Per Wired, 'one day in 2017' Noam Shazeer, at Google since 2000, overheard Vaswani and Niki Parmar while passing Lukasz Kaiser's workspace in Building 1965, joined, and rewrote the code; Uszkoreit said that until then the model, compared with LSTMs, 'wasn't better'. Wired gives no season.

Facebook AI Research's convolutional ConvS2S translation model (arXiv 1705.03122, 8 May 2017) was the number the Google team was trying to beat; Parmar recalled it had taken Facebook days to train and the Transformer a matter of hours.

The team worked in Google's Buildings 1945 and 1965 on Charleston Road, Mountain View, gravitating to 1965 because 'it had a better espresso machine in the micro-kitchen'; a second-floor room in 1965 had couches by a curtain whose pattern looked to Vaswani like synapses and neurons.

The New Yorker reports that at about 3 a.m. during the late sprint Vaswani told Aidan Gomez the work was 'going to be a huge deal' and 'bigger' than machine translation, while Gomez thought 'It's just machine translation'; this is remembered dialogue, not a transcript. The team was 'pushing flat out for twelve weeks'.

A couple of weeks before the deadline Parmar and Vaswani learned in the Google lobby that the model had passed 26 BLEU and phoned Uszkoreit, who was driving down from paragliding; Wired says he broke out an old bottle of champagne from his mountain expedition truck. Parmar's only quoted words are 'Jakob had some old champagne in his car.'

The NIPS 2017 paper deadline was Friday 19 May 2017, 20:00 UTC. Parmar recalled the English-French numbers came 'like, five minutes before we submitted'; Wired's narration says the paper went in 'with barely two minutes to spare'.

Llion Jones, born and raised in Wales, coined the title 'Attention Is All You Need' from the Beatles' 'All You Need Is Love': 'It literally took five seconds of thought. I didn't think they would use it.'

'Attention Is All You Need' (arXiv 1706.03762) was posted on 12 June 2017, submitted by Llion Jones, by eight Google authors (Vaswani, Shazeer, Parmar, Uszkoreit, Jones, Gomez, Kaiser, Polosukhin), and presented at NIPS 2017 in Long Beach, California; revisions ran to v7 (2 August 2023).

The paper's author footnote reads 'Equal contribution. Listing order is random.' and assigns roles: Uszkoreit proposed replacing RNNs with self-attention; Vaswani with Polosukhin designed and implemented the first Transformer models; Shazeer proposed scaled dot-product attention, multi-head attention and the parameter-free position representation; Parmar designed, implemented, tuned and evaluated countless variants; Jones built the initial codebase, efficient inference and visualizations; Kaiser and Gomez designed and implemented tensor2tensor.

Aidan Gomez was a University of Toronto undergraduate intern at Google Brain, aged 20 and too young to drink in the US; he later learned the internship was meant for PhD students. He had joined Hinton's lab as an undergraduate and grew up in an Ontario farming village where his family tapped maple trees.

The Transformer is an encoder-decoder with 6 encoder and 6 decoder layers, d_model = 512, 8 attention heads of size 64, feed-forward inner size 2048, residual connections with layer normalisation (post-LN), and Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QK^T/sqrt(d_k))V; the base model has about 65 million parameters and the big model (d_model 1024, 16 heads, d_ff 4096) 213 million.

The paper divides dot products by sqrt(d_k) because 'for large values of d_k, the dot products grow large in magnitude, pushing the softmax function into regions where it has extremely small gradients'; its footnote notes that for unit-variance components q.k has variance d_k.

The original Transformer used fixed sinusoidal positional encodings added to the embeddings, with wavelengths forming a geometric progression from 2pi to 10000*2pi; learned position embeddings gave 'nearly identical results' (25.7 vs 25.8 dev BLEU).
In the paper's ablations (EN-DE dev BLEU, base 25.8) one head scored 24.9, 'Single-head attention is 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting', 32 heads 25.4, no dropout 24.6.

On WMT 2014 the big Transformer scored 28.4 BLEU English-German (more than 2 BLEU over the best previous results including ensembles) and 41.8 English-French; the base model (27.3) beat every previous single model and ensemble (best 26.36). Base trained in 12 hours (100K steps) and big in 3.5 days (300K steps) on one machine with 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs.
By the paper's own estimates the base Transformer's training cost 3.3e18 FLOPs against 2.3e19 for Google's GNMT+RL, about one-seventh (a derived ratio).
Version 7 of the paper contains two English-French figures: 41.8 BLEU in the abstract and Table 2, and 41.0 in the text of section 6.1; the film should use 41.8 or omit the number.

The paper's Table 1 gives self-attention O(n^2 d) cost per layer with O(1) sequential operations and O(1) maximum path length, versus O(n) for both in recurrent layers; self-attention is cheaper than recurrence when sequence length n is smaller than representation size d, and its n^2 cost led the authors to float restricted local attention for long inputs.
A 4-layer Transformer reached 91.3 F1 on WSJ constituency parsing trained on about 40K sentences and 92.7 semi-supervised, an experiment Kaiser added to show the model was not just a translator.

Two weeks after the 3 a.m. conversation, with Gomez back in Toronto, Kaiser emailed him 'Generated Wikipedia Articles': a transformer given two days to read 'a little less than half' of Wikipedia had invented five plausible articles titled 'The Transformer', including a Japanese hardcore-punk band 'formed in 1968'. Gomez: 'I was shocked, blown away'.

Google's research blog announced the Transformer on 31 August 2017 (by Jakob Uszkoreit) and open-sourced Tensor2Tensor; it said that for 'I arrived at the bank after crossing the river' the model 'can learn to immediately attend to the word river'.

At the NIPS 2017 poster session in Long Beach on 6 December 2017 the crowd stayed until the 10:30 pm close ('Security had to tell us to leave'), and Sepp Hochreiter, co-inventor of the LSTM, praised the work.

The paper's Figures 3-5 show layer-5 encoder heads attending from 'making' to the distant 'more difficult', and two heads 'apparently involved in anaphora resolution' with attentions 'very sharp' for 'its'; the caption says 'The heads clearly learned to perform different tasks.'

Liu et al. (including Kaiser and Shazeer), 'Generating Wikipedia by Summarizing Long Sequences' (arXiv 30 January 2018), introduced 'a decoder-only architecture'; OpenAI's GPT-1 says it uses 'a multi-layer Transformer decoder [34]', citing that Google paper.

ELMo (Allen Institute for AI and University of Washington, arXiv 15 February 2018) used a 2-layer bidirectional LSTM, not a transformer, and was a NAACL 2018 Outstanding Paper; it was not the first pretrained contextual model, since CoVe (1 August 2017) and ULMFiT (18 January 2018) came earlier.

In spring 2018 Shazeer gave a talk titled 'Bigger Is Better' on scaling transformers; per Wired he had proposed that Google replace its search index with one huge transformer, an idea Kaiser at the time thought ridiculous.

OpenAI's GPT-1 (blog 11 June 2018; Radford, Narasimhan, Salimans, Sutskever) was a 12-layer decoder-only Transformer (768-dim, 12 heads) pretrained on BooksCorpus ('over 7,000 unique unpublished books') at a cost of '1 month on 8 GPUs', then fine-tuned, setting state of the art on 9 of 12 tasks.

Google's BERT (arXiv 11 October 2018; Devlin, Chang, Lee, Toutanova) was a bidirectional encoder-only Transformer (110M base, 340M large) trained by masking 15% of tokens on BooksCorpus plus English Wikipedia (3.3B words); it set records on eleven tasks (GLUE 80.4 in the October 2018 v1; 80.5 in the May 2019 v2); each pretraining took 4 days on up to 64 TPU chips; BERT-base was sized to match OpenAI GPT.

OpenAI announced GPT-2 on 14 February 2019: a 1.5-billion-parameter (paper: 1542M, 48 layers) decoder-only model trained to predict the next word on WebText, 40 GB from about 8 million web pages linked from Reddit posts with at least 3 karma; it reached state of the art on 7 of 8 language-modelling datasets zero-shot.

OpenAI withheld the full GPT-2 citing 'concerns about malicious applications' and released it in stages: a model it called '345M' in May 2019 (relabelled 355M by August), 774M on 20 August 2019 and the full 1.5B on 5 November 2019, when it wrote 'We've seen no strong evidence of misuse so far'; Cornell partners measured human-rated credibility of 6.91 (1.5B), 6.72 (774M) and 6.07 (355M) out of 10.

The phrase 'too dangerous to release' does not appear in OpenAI's 14 February 2019 post; the Guardian's headline the same day was 'New AI fake text generator may be too dangerous to release, say creators'. Who originated the framing is contested; safe wording is 'the press framed it as too dangerous to release'.

The Verge (21 February 2019) reported the backlash: Anima Anandkumar said withholding GPT-2 'put academics at a big disadvantage', Delip Rao said 'too dangerous' was 'casually thrown out', and OpenAI's Miles Brundage replied that 'it's important to distinguish what we said from what others said'.

OpenAI's GPT-2 post showcased a completion of a human-written prompt about 'a herd of unicorns living in a remote, previously unexplored valley, in the Andes Mountains' who 'spoke perfect English'; the post notes the sample took '10 tries'.
Google's T5 (arXiv 23 October 2019) cast every task as text-to-text, trained on the about-750 GB C4 corpus from Common Crawl, with models up to 11 billion parameters on TPU v3 pod slices.

On 25 October 2019 Google said BERT was helping it understand 'one in 10 searches in the U.S. in English', calling it 'the biggest leap forward in the past five years'; per Wired, Google had moved Translate to transformers in 2018.

Whether attention weights explain a model was debated: Jain and Wallace, 'Attention is not Explanation' (arXiv 26 February 2019, mostly on BiLSTM-with-attention classifiers); Clark et al. found BERT heads tracking syntax and coreference 'with remarkably high accuracy' (11 June 2019); Wiegreffe and Pinter replied 'Attention is not not Explanation' (13 August 2019).

Anthropic's Elhage et al., 'A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits' (22 December 2021), first named and described induction heads, a two-head circuit completing [A][B]...[A] -> [B]; Olsson et al. (8 March 2022) showed they form in a sudden phase change visible as a bump in training loss and may be 'the mechanism for the actual majority of all in-context learning in large transformer models', on evidence they call 'preliminary and indirect'.

Every ingredient of the Transformer had precedents (Bahdanau attention 2014, intra-attention 2016-17, residual connections, layer normalisation by Ba, Kiros and Hinton 2016); the paper's own claim is narrower: 'the first transduction model relying entirely on self-attention'.

Juergen Schmidhuber argues 1991-era 'fast weight programmers' are equivalent to linear (unnormalised) self-attention (Schlag, Irie and Schmidhuber 2021); mainstream credit for softmax self-attention and the 2017 architecture goes to Vaswani et al. Present as a claim, not a settled priority.

Whether Google 'missed' its own invention is disputed: Sam Altman told Wired 'I don't think anyone at Google realized what it meant' and Uszkoreit asked 'why didn't we do anything with the fact that we had seen it?'; on the other side Google shipped transformers in Translate (2018) and BERT in Search (2019).

Jakob Uszkoreit's father, the computational linguist Hans Uszkoreit, had been jailed for 15 months in East Germany for protesting the 1968 Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia; he doubted self-attention at the dinner table and later co-founded a company building language models 'using transformers, of course'.
Google colleague Mat Kelcey, who told Llion Jones about self-attention, doubted it would work: 'basically the biggest incorrect prediction of my life'.

By March 2024 all eight authors had left Google (Wired): Gomez co-founded Cohere (Toronto, 2019); Shazeer co-founded Character.AI (October 2021); Vaswani and Parmar co-founded Adept then Essential AI; Jones co-founded Sakana AI (Tokyo); Uszkoreit co-founded Inceptive (RNA biotech); Polosukhin co-founded NEAR; Kaiser joined OpenAI, the only one not to found a company.

Google rehired Shazeer from Character.AI in a licensing deal announced 2 August 2024 and he became a Gemini co-lead; Reuters, CNBC and Axios headlines of 17-18 June 2026 report he left Google for OpenAI. The 2023 risk debate split three ways: existential-risk worriers (CAIS, FLI, Hinton, Bengio, Yudkowsky), present-harms critics (the DAIR authors), and sceptics of doom (LeCun); the three 2018 Turing laureates split two (Hinton, Bengio) to one (LeCun). People also overlapped: Hinton named bad actors and job loss as well as takeover.

Anthropic published its Responsible Scaling Policy on 19 September 2023, defining AI Safety Levels 'modeled loosely after the US government's biosafety level (BSL) standards', from ASL-1 (no meaningful catastrophic risk) to ASL-3 (substantially increased risk of catastrophic misuse or low-level autonomous capabilities).

President Biden signed Executive Order 14110 on 30 October 2023, requiring reports on models trained with more than 10^26 operations (10^23 for models trained mainly on biological sequences) and on clusters above 10^20 operations per second; it was revoked on 20 January 2025 by EO 14148.

The Bletchley Declaration (AI Safety Summit, Bletchley Park, 1-2 November 2023), a political declaration rather than a treaty, was signed by 28 countries and the EU including both the United States and China, warning of 'potential for serious, even catastrophic, harm'; New Zealand joined on 23 October 2024.

China's Interim Measures for the Management of Generative AI Services (CAC Order No. 15; seven agencies; 24 articles) were published 13 July 2023 and took effect 15 August 2023; they apply to services offered to the public in the PRC, state 'equal weight to development and security' (Art. 3) and require adherence to 'core socialist values' (Art. 4).

Why Altman was removed remains disputed: the board's only public reason was candour; later reporting cites concerns over safety, commercialisation and candour (including that employee concerns were led by Sutskever and Murati, which was not public in November 2023); Helen Toner said in May 2024 that Altman had withheld information; the WilmerHale review (March 2024) found his conduct 'did not mandate removal'; 'Q*' speculation was never confirmed.

Hinton learned of his share of the 2024 Physics Nobel (with John Hopfield, then 91) at about 2 a.m. in 'a cheap hotel in California' with no internet, had planned an MRI that day, and first wondered whether it was 'a spoof call'; committee chair Ellen Moons said the laureates 'used fundamental concepts from statistical physics', while Dame Wendy Hall called it 'a bit of a stretch'.

Whether the 2024 Physics Nobel was 'physics' was debated: the committee pointed to the Hopfield network's energy function and the Boltzmann machine's statistical physics; Wendy Hall asked whether the work was 'the result of physics research'.
